```{r set-options}

#| warning: true

options(
  pillar.sigfig = 5,
  # (Twomey, 2026)
  scipen = 999
)
```

:::

#== display records ==

The modeling dataset loads with *15,766* records and *35* columns, matching the size saved by the cleaning script.

<br>

## Build a rough model

Before building the full model, a quick weather-only model checks that everything 
runs. Agency population and jurisdiction location are added later, after the missing population values are filled. The code follows examples from DataSciencePlus.com 
*"Base R glm() vs tidymodels for Logistic Regression: What You Actually Gain"*, 
the TidyModels.org article *"Preprocess your data with recipes,"* and R-Statistics.co's *"parsnip fit() in R: Train a Model Specification"* (Example 4).

```{r prototype-weather-model}
#| label: 02-prototype-weather-model
#| warning: true

# Verify logistic regression runs with the four weather features.

#== set the outcome order ==
homicide_modeling_df <- homicide_modeling_df %>%
  mutate(
    victim_racial_construct = factor(
      victim_racial_construct,
      levels = c(
        "Not Black",
        "Black"
      )
    )
  )

#== display counts ==
homicide_modeling_df %>%
  count(victim_racial_construct) %>%
  # (Muldoon, 2021)
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = md("**Female Victim Racial Class**")
  )

#== fit the model ==
# (Dhana, 2026; Prabhakaran, 2026f)
weather_fit_poc <- logistic_reg() %>%
  set_engine(
    "glm"
  ) %>%
  # (Dhana, 2026)
  parsnip::fit(
    victim_racial_construct ~
      temp_2m_avg +
      relative_humidity_2m_avg +
      rain_sum +
      snowfall_sum,
    data = homicide_modeling_df
  )

#== coefficient table + p-values ==
weather_fit_poc %>%
  # (Dhana, 2026; Datanovia, 2026a)
  broom::tidy() %>%
  # (Andrzej, 2020)
  mutate_if(
    is.numeric,
    round,
    5
  ) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  # (Muldoon, 2021)
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = md("**Rough Model: Coefficient + Z-value + P-value**"),
    subtitle = md("weather predictor table")
  )

#== convergence check ==
# (Prabhakaran, 2026f)
extract_fit_engine(
  weather_fit_poc
)$converged

#== predicted class split ==
# (Datanovia, 2026a)
weather_fit_poc %>%
  predict(
    new_data = homicide_modeling_df
  ) %>%
  count(
    # (Dhana, 2026)
    .pred_class
  ) %>%
  # (Muldoon, 2021)
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = md("**Predicted Female Class Split**"),
    subtitle = md("*are black v/s predicted black*")
  )
```

After running, the model showed that it converged. It predicted 4.5% of victims as Black, while 35.7% actually are, so it predicts Black far less often than it occurs. This is only a check, and the full model with agency population and jurisdiction location comes next.

:::

<br>

## Training & testing set

Before the full model is built, the records are split into a training set (11,824 of the records) for building the model and a testing set (the remaining 3,942) for checking how it does on records it hasn't seen. The split keeps the share of Black victims about the same in both sets.

#### split the data

```{r split-data}
#| label: 02-split-data
#| warning: true

# Split the modeling data into training and testing sets.

#== set the seed ==
set.seed(2026)

#== reproducible split ==
homicide_split <- homicide_modeling_df %>%
  # (Prabhakaran, 2026g; Datanovia, 2026a; Dhana, 2026)
  initial_split(
    prop = 3 / 4,
    strata = victim_racial_construct
  )

#== train/test split data ==
homicide_train <- homicide_split %>%
  # (Datanovia, 2026a; Dhana, 2026)
  training()

homicide_test <- homicide_split %>%
  # (Datanovia, 2026a; Dhana, 2026)
  testing()

#== call the total rows function ==
# (Buck, 2025)
total_rows(
  `Training n()` = homicide_train,
  `Testing n()` = homicide_test
)

#== display outcome mix ==
homicide_train %>%
  count(
    victim_racial_construct
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    prop = n / sum(n)
  ) %>%
  # (Muldoon, 2021)
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = md("**Training Model Outcome**"),
    subtitle = md("*totals and proportions*")
  )

homicide_test %>%
  count(
    victim_racial_construct
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    prop = n / sum(n)
  ) %>%
  # (Muldoon, 2021)
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = md("**Testing Model Outcome**"),
    subtitle = md("*totals and proportions*")
  )
```

As you can see, both sets have nearly the same mix: *0.64318* Not Black and *0.35682* Black in the training set, and *0.64307* Not Black and *0.35693* Black in the testing set, close to the full dataset. The model will be built on the training set only, and the testing set stays untouched until the model is evaluated.

<br>

## Training set

The recipe lists the outcome and the six predictors. It fills the missing agency population values with the median from the training set, and turns jurisdiction location into a 0/1 column the model can read.

#### build recipe

```{r build-recipe}
#| label: 02-build-recipe
#| warning: true

# Specify the preprocessing steps, and set up the outcome and the six predictors.

#== build the recipe ==
# (Dhana, 2026; Datanovia, 2026a)
homicide_recipe <- recipes::recipe(
  victim_racial_construct ~
    temp_2m_avg +
    relative_humidity_2m_avg +
    rain_sum +
    snowfall_sum +
    agency_population +
    jurisdiction_match,
  data = homicide_train
) %>%
  #== learn the median ==
  # (Dhana, 2026)
  recipes::step_impute_median(
    agency_population
  ) %>%
  #== encode factors ==
  # (Dhana, 2026)
  recipes::step_dummy(
    recipes::all_nominal_predictors()
  )

#== display recipe ==
homicide_recipe
```

#### fit the full model

The recipe and the logistic regression are bundled into one workflow and fit on the training set, so the same steps will be applied when the model is checked on the testing set.

```{r fit-full-model}
#| label: 02-fit-full-model
#| warning: true

# Fit the full logistic regression on the training set.

#== bundle steps ==
# (Datanovia, 2026a; Dhana, 2026)
full_fit <- workflows::workflow() %>%
  #== glue the recipe ==
  workflows::add_recipe(
    homicide_recipe
  ) %>%
  #== glue the model ==
  workflows::add_model(
    # (Dhana, 2026; Prabhakaran, 2026f)
    logistic_reg() %>%
      set_engine(
        "glm"
      )
  ) %>%
  # (Dhana, 2026)
  parsnip::fit(
    data = homicide_train
  )

#== coefficient table + p-values ==
full_fit %>%
  # (Dhana, 2026; Datanovia, 2026a)
  broom::tidy() %>%
  # (Andrzej, 2020)
  mutate_if(
    is.numeric,
    round,
    5
  ) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  # (Muldoon, 2021)
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = md("**Full Model: Coefficient + Z-value + P-value**"),
    subtitle = md("*full predictor table*")
  )

#== convergence check ==
# (Prabhakaran, 2026f)
workflowsets::extract_fit_engine(
  full_fit
)$converged
```

The full model converged (TRUE). Five predictors have positive estimates: temperature, humidity, rain, agency population, and Within Jurisdiction. Higher values for these predictors are associated with a greater chance that the victim is Black. Records from Within Jurisdiction are also more likely to involve a Black victim than records from the Surrounding Area. Snowfall has a negative estimate. All six predictors have p-values below .05. The model’s performance on the testing set is discussed next.

<br>

## Testing set

::: {.content-hidden when-profile="book"}

Now the testing set is used for the first time. The fitted workflow applies the same recipe and model to the 3,942 testing records, so the model is checked on records it hasn't seen.

```{r predict-test-set}
#| label: 02-predict-test-set
#| warning: true

# Predict the outcome for the testing set with the fitted workflow.

#== bind predictions to test set ==
test_results <- full_fit %>%
  # (Dhana, 2026)
  augment(
    new_data = homicide_test
  )

#== display test set ==
test_results %>%
  select(
    victim_racial_construct,
    .pred_class,
    `.pred_Not Black`,
    .pred_Black
  ) %>%
  head() %>%
  # (Muldoon, 2021)
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = md("**Binded Predictions**"),
    subtitle = md("*from fitted model*")
  )

#== count predicted categories ==
test_results %>%
  count(
    # (Dhana, 2026)
    .pred_class
  ) %>%
  # (Muldoon, 2021)
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = md("**Model Outcome Levels**"),
    subtitle = md("*counts*")
  )
```

The testing set kept all *3,942* records and now has *38* columns because the `augment()` added three: the predicted class and the two predicted probabilities, one for each outcome level. The model predicted Not Black for *3,669* records and Black for *273*, while the testing set has *1,407* Black victims. So the model rarely gives Black a predicted probability above the classification cutoff (*0.5*), even though about a third of the testing victims are Black. How often these predictions are right is checked next.

:::

#### evaluate metrics

Now it's time to score the predictions against the benchmarks set before testing, an accuracy above the *64.3%* always Not Black baseline and a ROC AUC above *0.5*, along with sensitivity, specificity, and the J-index to show how well each outcome level is identified.

```{r evaluate-metrics}
#| label: 02-evaluate-metrics
#| warning: true

# Score the testing-set predictions with different performance metrics.

#== bundle metrics ==
# (Twomey, 2026)
homicide_metrics <- metric_set(
  roc_auc,
  accuracy,
  yardstick::sensitivity,
  yardstick::specificity,
  j_index
)

#== calculate metrics ==
test_results %>%
  homicide_metrics(
    # (Twomey, 2026)
    truth = victim_racial_construct,
    estimate = .pred_class,
    .pred_Black,
    event_level = "second"
  ) %>%
  # (Muldoon, 2021)
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = md("**Predictions Performance Metrics**"),
    subtitle = md("*before testing*")
  )
```

The model's accuracy is *0.63978*, which is below the *0.64307* baseline, and its ROC AUC is *0.64748*, which is above *0.5*. Sensitivity is *0.092395*, specificity is *0.94359*, and the J-index is *0.035985*, so the model correctly labels most Not Black victims but identifies few Black victims. Because both benchmarks had to be met, the model does not meet the success criterion.

::: {.content-hidden when-profile="book"}

<br>

## Coefficients

The coefficients in the full model are on the log-odds scale, so here they're converted to odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals, and each predictor's p-value is compared with alpha (.05) to test the null hypothesis.

```{r odds-ratios}
#| label: 02-odds-ratios
#| warning: true

# Convert the full model's coefficients to odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals.

#== odds ratios + 95% CIs ==
full_fit %>%
  # (Datanovia, 2026a; Dhana, 2026)
  broom::tidy(
    exponentiate = TRUE,
    conf.int = TRUE
  ) %>%
  #== keep the reported columns ==
  # (Dhana, 2026)
  select(
    term,
    aOR = estimate,
    conf.low,
    conf.high,
    p.value
  ) %>%
  #== formatted table ==
  # (Andrzej, 2020)
  mutate_if(
    is.numeric,
    round,
    5
  ) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  # (Muldoon, 2021)
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = md("**Adjusted Odds Ratios**"),
    subtitle = md("*with 95% CIs*")
  )
```

The adjusted odds ratios (aOR) point the same way as the estimates in the full model. Five predictors have an aOR above 1: 

|  Predictor              | Odds Ratio (OR) | 95% Confidence Interval (CI) |
|:-----------------------:|:---------------:|:----------------------------:|
| temperature             | *1.00357*       | *1.00064* to *1.00650*       |
| humidity                | *1.02800*       | *1.02356* to *1.03250*       |
| rain                    | *1.03704*       | *1.01810* to *1.05646*       |
| agency population       | *1.00003*       | *1.00002* to *1.00004*       |

> _jurisdiction location, where records *"Within Jurisdiction"* have *1.23549* times the odds of those in the *"Surrounding Area"* (95% CI *1.11543* to *1.36953*)._ 

Snowfall is the only one below 1 (*0.96867*, 95% CI *0.95692* to *0.98009*). Agency population's aOR shows a very small but real change in the odds for each additional person served.

For the predictor's p-value they all are below alpha (.05): 

|  Predictor                         | Probability Value (p-value)  |
|:----------------------------------:|:----------------------------:|
| temperature                        | *0.01662*                    |
| rain                               | *0.00012*                    |
| Within Jurisdiction                | *0.00005*                    |

> _humidity, snowfall, and agency population (p < .00001, printed as *0.00000*)_

None of the 95% confidence intervals include 1, which agrees with the p-values, so I reject the null hypothesis for all six predictors. The intercept isn't a predictor, so it isn't part of this test. Even so, the model's accuracy on the testing set (*0.63978*) fell below the *0.64307* baseline, so the predictors are linked to whether the victim is Black, but not strongly enough to classify individual victims better than always guessing Not Black.

:::

<br>

## Practical significance

::: {.content-hidden when-profile="book"}

The p-values show that every predictor is associated with the outcome, but they don’t indicate whether each association is large enough to matter. To assess this, I'll compare the change in the expected proportion of Black victims for each predictor with the 5.5-point difference between the two jurisdiction groups identified in the exploratory analysis. First, I'll calculate the 1st quartile, median, and 3rd quartile of each numeric predictor in the training set. These values represent low, middle, and high values for each predictor and will show how much the expected proportion of Black victims changes as each predictor moves from low to high.

```{r predictor-quartiles}
#| label: 02-predictor-quartiles
#| warning: true

# Find each predictor's 1st quartile, median, and 3rd quartile in the training set.

#== quartiles ==
predictor_quartiles <- homicide_train %>%
  select(
    temp_2m_avg,
    relative_humidity_2m_avg,
    rain_sum,
    snowfall_sum,
    agency_population
  ) %>%
  # (Olumide, 2025)
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "predictor",
    values_to = "value"
  ) %>%
  group_by(
    predictor
  ) %>%
  rename(
    `Predictor` = predictor
  ) %>%
  summarise(
    `1st Quartile` = quantile(
      value,
      0.25,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    `Median` = median(
      value,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    `3rd Quartile` = quantile(
      value,
      0.75,
      na.rm = TRUE
    )
  )

#== display quartiles ==
predictor_quartiles %>%
  # (Muldoon, 2021)
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = md("**Predictors' Measures of Positions**")
  )
```

The hypothetical records will use the training set's medians: a temperature of *60.887* °F, humidity of *70.233*%, rainfall of *2.839* inches, snowfall of *0* inches, and an agency population of *393*. Snowfall's 1st quartile and median are both *0*, and its 3rd quartile is only *0.55125* inches, since at least half of the training records come from months with no snowfall.

Then, because the odds ratios describe changes in the odds rather than in percentage points, I'll build two hypothetical records that differ only in jurisdiction location, holding the weather and agency population at their medians, and predict the proportion of Black victims for each, so I can compare jurisdiction's effect with the 5.5-point difference seen in the exploratory analysis.

```{r jurisdiction-practical}
#| label: 02-jurisdiction-practical
#| warning: true

# Predict the proportion of Black victims for each jurisdiction group.

#== predictor records ==
# (Posit team, n.d.)
jurisdiction_points <- expand.grid(
  temp_2m_avg = 60.887,
  relative_humidity_2m_avg = 70.233,
  rain_sum = 2.839,
  snowfall_sum = 0,
  agency_population = 393,
  jurisdiction_match = c(
    "Surrounding Area",
    "Within Jurisdiction"
  )
)

#== predicted proportions ==
jurisdiction_predictions <- full_fit %>%
  # (Dhana, 2026)
  augment(
    new_data = jurisdiction_points
  ) %>%
  select(
    jurisdiction_match,
    .pred_Black
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    percent_black = round(
      100 * .pred_Black,
      1
    ),
    # (Wong, 2026)
    changed = "jurisdiction_match",
    # (Datanovia, 2026b)
    group = c(
      "Low",
      "High"
    )
  )

#== display table ==
jurisdiction_predictions %>%
  # (Muldoon, 2021)
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = md("**Predictor per Jurisdiction Class Table**"),
    subtitle = md("*surrounding area v/s within jurisdiction*")
  )
```

With the weather and agency population held at their medians, the model predicts that *33.2*% of Surrounding Area records and *38.0*% of Within Jurisdiction records are Black, a difference of about *4.8* percentage points. This is smaller than the 5.5-point difference seen in the exploratory analysis, so jurisdiction location on its own falls below the practical-significance cutoff, even though it is statistically significant.

:::

#### predictor practicalness

Next, since the numeric predictors don't have groups, I'll build two hypothetical records for each one that differ only in that predictor, one at its 1st quartile and one at its 3rd quartile. The other numeric predictors stay at their medians, and jurisdiction location is set to Within Jurisdiction, the group with most of the records. Then I'll predict the proportion of Black victims for each record and compare each predictor's change with the 5.5-point difference.

```{r predictor-practical}
#| label: 02-predictor-practical
#| warning: true

# Predict the proportion of Black victims as each numeric predictor rises from the first to third quartile.

#== records of predictor change ==
quartile_points <- bind_rows(
  # (Posit team, n.d.)
  expand.grid(
    changed = "temp_2m_avg",
    temp_2m_avg = c(
      46.506,
      73.023
    ),
    relative_humidity_2m_avg = 70.233,
    rain_sum = 2.839,
    snowfall_sum = 0,
    agency_population = 393,
    jurisdiction_match = "Within Jurisdiction"
  ),
  # (Posit team, n.d.)
  expand.grid(
    changed = "relative_humidity_2m_avg",
    temp_2m_avg = 60.887,
    relative_humidity_2m_avg = c(
      62.548,
      74.968
    ),
    rain_sum = 2.839,
    snowfall_sum = 0,
    agency_population = 393,
    jurisdiction_match = "Within Jurisdiction"
  ),
  # (Posit team, n.d.)
  expand.grid(
    changed = "rain_sum",
    temp_2m_avg = 60.887,
    relative_humidity_2m_avg = 70.233,
    rain_sum = c(
      1.213,
      4.6185
    ),
    snowfall_sum = 0,
    agency_population = 393,
    jurisdiction_match = "Within Jurisdiction"
  ),
  # (Posit team, n.d.)
  expand.grid(
    changed = "snowfall_sum",
    temp_2m_avg = 60.887,
    relative_humidity_2m_avg = 70.233,
    rain_sum = 2.839,
    snowfall_sum = c(
      0,
      0.55125
    ),
    agency_population = 393,
    jurisdiction_match = "Within Jurisdiction"
  ),
  # (Posit team, n.d.)
  expand.grid(
    changed = "agency_population",
    temp_2m_avg = 60.887,
    relative_humidity_2m_avg = 70.233,
    rain_sum = 2.839,
    snowfall_sum = 0,
    agency_population = c(
      99,
      1760
    ),
    jurisdiction_match = "Within Jurisdiction"
  )
)

#== predicted proportions ==
quartile_predictions <- full_fit %>%
  # (Dhana, 2026)
  augment(
    new_data = quartile_points
  ) %>%
  select(
    changed,
    .pred_Black
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    percent_black = round(
      100 * .pred_Black,
      1
    ),
    # (Datanovia, 2026b)
    group = rep(
      c(
        "Low",
        "High"
      ),
      times = 5
    )
  )

#== display table ==
quartile_predictions %>%
  # (Muldoon, 2021)
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = md("**Predictor Proportion Change Table**"),
    subtitle = md("*within jurisdiction only*")
  )
```

Moving each numeric predictor from its 1st to its 3rd quartile changes the predicted proportion of Black victims by about *2.2* percentage points for temperature, *8.0* for humidity, *2.9* for rainfall, *-0.4* for snowfall, and *1.2* for agency population. Only humidity changes the proportion by more than the 5.5-point difference, so humidity is the only predictor large enough to count as practically significant by this cutoff, while the others are statistically significant but fall below it.

<br>

## Model visuals

::: {.content-hidden when-profile="book"}

##### Calibration Curve

Next, I'll plot the model's calibration curve on the testing set. The predictions are split into ten equal-size bins, and each bin's average predicted probability of Black is compared with the actual proportion of Black victims in that bin, so the curve shows whether the model's probabilities match what actually happened.

```{r calibration-curve-fx}
#| label: 02-calibration-curve-fx
#| warning: true

# Call the calibration-curve function from the utils script.

#== calibration table ==
# (Buck, 2025)
calibration_table <- calibration_data(
  test_results$.pred_Black,
  test_results$victim_racial_construct == "Black",
  "Full model"
)

#== display bins ==
calibration_table %>%
  # (Muldoon, 2021)
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = md("**Calibration Curve Outcomes**"),
    subtitle = md("*full model*")
  )
```

```{r calibration-curve-plot}
#| label: 02-calibration-curve-plot
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 11

# Plot the testing set's calibration curve for the full model.

#== plot calibration curve ==
# (Wong, 2026)
calibration_plot <- calibration_table %>%
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = mean_pred,
      y = observed_rate,
      color = model
    )
  ) +
  geom_point(
    size = 2.10,
    color = "#275561"
  ) +
  geom_line(
    size = 1.55,
    color = "#275561"
  ) +
  geom_abline(
    slope = 1,
    intercept = 0,
    size = 1.5,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "#9D5E38"
  ) +
  coord_equal(
    xlim = c(
      0,
      1
    ),
    ylim = c(
      0,
      1
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Mean predicted probability",
    y = "Observed event rate",
    title = "Calibration of the full model",
    subtitle = "on testing set",
    caption = "Fig.6"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  ggplot_theme

#== display figure 6 ==
calibration_plot

#== save figure ==
ggsave(
  # (Olumide, 2025)

```

The model's average predicted probability of being Black ranges from *0.17436* in the lowest bin to *0.54855* in the highest. Only the highest bin’s average exceeds the 0.5 classification cutoff, helping explain why the model classified just *273* testing records as Black. In bins 6 through 9, the points fall above the diagonal (e.g., bin 8 has a predicted value of *0.42029* and an observed value of *0.48477*), indicating that the model underpredicts the proportion of Black victims in those bins. Bins 1, 2, and 10 fall below the diagonal.

## Odds ratios

:::

Then, I'll plot each predictor's odds ratio with its 95% confidence interval as a forest plot. Because the numeric predictors are measured in different units, such as one person, one degree, or one inch, I'll scale each numeric predictor's odds ratio and confidence interval to its quartile range, the change from its 1st to its 3rd quartile (pakalla, 2020; Noah, 2020), so every odds ratio describes the same low-to-high change used in the practical-significance check. Jurisdiction location stays as is, comparing Within Jurisdiction with Surrounding Area.

::: {.content-hidden when-profile="book"}

```{r odds-ratio-forest}
#| label: 02-odds-ratio-forest
#| warning: false

# Build each predictor's odds ratio per quartile-range increase, with Wald 95% confidence intervals.

#== quartile ranges ==
quartile_ranges <- predictor_quartiles %>%
  mutate(
    iqr = c(
      `3rd Quartile` - `1st Quartile`
    )
  ) %>%
  select(
    Predictor,
    iqr
  )

#== scaled odds ratios ==
odds_ratio_table <- full_fit %>%
  # (Masum, 2026d)
  broom::tidy(
    exponentiate = TRUE
  ) %>%
  # (Masum, 2026d; Wickham et al., 2026d)
  filter(
    term != "(Intercept)"
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    quartile_ranges,
    by = c(
      "term" = "Predictor"
    )
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    # (Matt, 2020; Hadley, 2024)
    iqr = case_when(
      is.na(iqr) ~ 1,
      TRUE ~ iqr
    ),
    # (Masum, 2026d)
    conf.low = exp(
      # (Masum, 2026a)
      iqr *
        # (Masum, 2026d)
        (log(estimate) - 1.96 * std.error)
    ),
    # (Masum, 2026d)
    conf.high = exp(
      # (Masum, 2026a)
      iqr *
        # (Masum, 2026d)
        (log(estimate) + 1.96 * std.error)
    ),
    # (Masum, 2026a)
    estimate = exp(
      iqr * log(estimate)
    ),
    # (Matt, 2020; Hadley, 2024)
    term = case_when(
      term == "temp_2m_avg" ~ "Temperature",
      term == "relative_humidity_2m_avg" ~ "Relative humidity",
      term == "rain_sum" ~ "Rainfall",
      term == "snowfall_sum" ~ "Snowfall",
      term == "agency_population" ~ "Agency population",
      term ==
        "jurisdiction_match_Within.Jurisdiction" ~ "Within Jurisdiction vs. Surrounding Area"
    ),
    # (Masum, 2026d)
    significant = p.value < 0.05
  )

#== display scaled odds ratios ==
odds_ratio_table %>%
  # (Masum, 2026b; Masum, 2026a)
  dplyr::select(
    term,
    iqr,
    estimate,
    conf.low,
    conf.high,
    p.value
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    across(
      c(
        iqr,
        estimate,
        conf.low,
        conf.high
      ),
      \(x) round(x, 3)
    ),
    p.value = format.pval(
      p.value,
      digits = 3
    )
  ) %>%
  # (Muldoon, 2021)
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = md("**Scaled Odds Ratios**"),
    subtitle = md("*1st to 3rd quartile, Wald 95% CI*")
  )
```

:::

#### odds ratio forest plot

```{r odds-ratio-forest-plot}
#| label: 02-odds-ratio-forest-plot
#| warning: true
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 7

# Plot the odds ratio.

#== forest plot ==
# (Masum, 2026b)
odds_ratio_plot <- ggplot(
  odds_ratio_table,
  aes(
    x = estimate,
    y = reorder(term, estimate),
    color = significant
  )
) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 1,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "#FFB060"
  ) +
  # (Masum, 2026c)
  geom_pointrange(
    aes(
      xmin = conf.low,
      xmax = conf.high
    ),
    size = 0.8,
    linewidth = 1.1
  ) +
  # (Masum, 2026d)
  geom_text(
    aes(
      label = sprintf("OR = %.2f", estimate)
    ),
    vjust = -1,
    size = 3.8,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  # (Masum, 2026d)
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "TRUE" = "#275561",
      "FALSE" = "grey60"
    ),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  # (Masum, 2026d)
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(
    x = "Odds ratio (log scale)",
    y = NULL,
    title = "Odds ratios for each predictor",
    subtitle = "1st to 3rd quartile (Surrounding Area to Within Jurisdiction),\n95% CI on log scale; teal = p < 0.05",
    caption = "Fig.7"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  ggplot_theme

#== display figure 7 ==
odds_ratio_plot

#== save figure ==
ggsave(
  # (Olumide, 2025)
  filename = here::here(
    "output",
    "figures",
    "fig_7.png"
  ),
  plot = odds_ratio_plot,
  width = 12,
  height = 7
)
```

Scaled to each predictor's quartile range, all six 95% confidence intervals exclude 1, indicating that every predictor is statistically significant at an alpha of .05, consistent with the p-values in the odds-ratios chunk. Relative humidity has the largest odds ratio: *1.409* (*1.335* to *1.487*) for a *12.419*-point increase. Snowfall is the only predictor with an odds ratio below 1: *0.983* (*0.976* to *0.989*) for a *0.551*-inch increase. The jurisdiction location interval (*1.115* to *1.369*) differs from the interval in the odds-ratios table by less than 0.001. The predictors rank in the same order as the practical-significance changes, with humidity showing the largest increase and snowfall the only decrease.

<br>

## Predicted Proportions

Finally, I'll show the practical-significance results in a paired plot. For each predictor, a line connects the predicted proportion of Black victims at its low value (1st quartile, or Surrounding Area for jurisdiction location) to the predicted proportion at its high value (3rd quartile, or Within Jurisdiction). The steeper the line, the greater the change in the expected proportion associated with that predictor.

::: {.content-hidden when-profile="book"}

First, the previously saved predictions, including the jurisdiction pair and five quartile pairs, are combined into one table. Each row is labeled with its predictor and as Low or High, allowing the two values for each predictor to be connected by a line.

```{r practical-significance}
#| label: 02-practical-significance
#| warning: true

# Build the predicted proportion data and a table.

#== paired data ==
# (Wong, 2026)
practical_long <- bind_rows(
  jurisdiction_predictions,
  quartile_predictions
) %>%
  mutate(
    # (Matt, 2020; Hadley, 2024)
    id = factor(
      case_when(
        changed == "jurisdiction_match" ~ "Jurisdiction location",
        changed == "temp_2m_avg" ~ "Temperature",
        changed == "relative_humidity_2m_avg" ~ "Relative humidity",
        changed == "rain_sum" ~ "Rainfall",
        changed == "snowfall_sum" ~ "Snowfall",
        changed == "agency_population" ~ "Agency population"
      )
    ),
    # (Datanovia, 2026b)
    group = factor(
      group,
      levels = c(
        "Low",
        "High"
      )
    )
  ) %>%
  select(
    id,
    group,
    percent_black
  )

#== build table ==
practical_long_table <- practical_long %>%
  # (Muldoon, 2021)
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = md("**Predictor Proportion Changes**"),
    subtitle = md("*from 1st quartile to 3rd quartile*")
  )

#== display table ==
practical_long_table
```

:::

#### practical significance plot

```{r practical-significance-plot}
#| label: 02-practical-significance-plot
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 8

# Plot each predictor's predicted proportion of Black victims from low to high.

#== paired plot ==
# (Datanovia, 2026b; stefan, 2022)
practical_plot <- ggpubr::ggpaired(
  practical_long,
  x = "group",
  y = "percent_black",
  # (Hervé, 2017)
  id = "id",
  order = c(
    "Low",
    "High"
  ),
  fill = "group",
  color = "group",
  palette = c(
    "Low" = "#9d5e38",
    "High" = "#5e2e11"
  ),
  # (L Tyrone, 2024)
  line.color = NA,
  # (Datanovia, 2026b; stefan, 2022)
  xlab = "Predictor value",
  ylab = "Predicted Black victims (%)"
) +
  # (stefan, 2022; russhh, 2017)
  geom_line(
    aes(
      group = id,
      color = id,
      linetype = id,
      linewidth = id
    )
  ) +
  # (russhh, 2017)
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      "Relative humidity" = "#275561",
      "Jurisdiction location" = "#5497a8",
      "Temperature" = "#70868c",
      "Rainfall" = "#cff5ff",
      "Snowfall" = "#0e6e87",
      "Agency population" = "#10302E"
    )
  ) +
  # (Wickham et al., 2026)
  scale_linetype_manual(
    values = c(
      "Relative humidity" = "solid",
      "Jurisdiction location" = "dashed",
      "Temperature" = "dotted",
      "Rainfall" = "dotdash",
      "Snowfall" = "longdash",
      "Agency population" = "twodash"
    )
  ) +
  # (Wickham et al., 2026)
  scale_linewidth_manual(
    values = c(
      "Relative humidity" = 1.6,
      "Jurisdiction location" = 1.3,
      "Temperature" = 0.95,
      "Rainfall" = 0.95,
      "Snowfall" = 0.95,
      "Agency population" = 1.2
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Change in the predicted proportion of Black victims",
    subtitle = "Each line joins one predictor's low and high value",
    caption = "Fig.8",
    fill = "Predictor value",
    colour = "Predictor",
    linetype = "Predictor",
    linewidth = "Predictor"
  ) +
  ggplot_theme

#== display figure 8 ==
practical_plot

#== save figure ==
ggsave(
  # (Olumide, 2025)
  filename = here::here(
    "output",
    "figures",
    "fig_8.png"
  ),
  plot = practical_plot,
  width = 12,
  height = 8
)
```

According to this plot, relative humidity has the steepest line, rising from *33.2*% at its 1st quartile to *41.2*% at its 3rd quartile, the only change larger than the 5.5-point difference. Jurisdiction location rises from *33.2*% to *38.0*%, and the other numeric predictors change by less, while snowfall's line is the only one that falls, from *38.0*% to *37.6*%. So the plot shows the same result as the practical-significance check: humidity is the only predictor whose change is large enough to count as practically significant.

<br>

## Conclusion

All six predictors are statistically significant, but the full model's testing-set accuracy (*0.63978*) fell below the *0.64307* always-"Not Black" baseline even though its ROC AUC (*0.64748*) was above *0.5*, so it does not meet the success criterion. Of the six predictors, only relative humidity changes the predicted proportion of Black victims by more than the 5.5-point difference, making it the only one that is also practically significant.

<br>
